title: Parashurama's challenge
hook: the wedding party is riding home when the sky goes dark and a man with an axe steps onto the road
carry: string this one, then we fight

segments.voice: Yesterday: four couples circled one fire, and Janaka gave Sita to Rama as his companion in dharma. Your line was a companion on the way.

It should be a caravan of pure joy. King Dasharatha, his four sons, four new daughters-in-law, priests, soldiers and wagons of gifts from King Janaka, all rolling back toward Ayodhya. Then the birds begin to cry harshly. At the same moment, deer pass by on the right, a good sign. The king is worried, and Vasishtha reads the signs for him: something frightening is coming, and it will pass. A wind rises. The ground shakes. Dust hides the sun. And out of the dark walks a man with an axe on his shoulder.
screen: `A CARAVAN OF PURE JOY.` → `BAD BIRDS, GOOD DEER.` → `A MAN WITH AN AXE.`

segments.voice: Valmiki describes him like a fire no one can look at straight: matted hair, a bow in one hand, an arrow in the other, the axe across his shoulder. He's the son of the sage Jamadagni, from the family of Bhrigu. Later tradition calls him Parashurama, Rama with the axe, and counts him among the avatars of Vishnu. He's a brahmin, a priest's son, who took up weapons. After his father was killed in a feud with a royal house, the stories say, he made war on the warrior class again and again. Now he has heard that a young prince named Rama broke Shiva's great bow. So he's brought a bow of his own, and a story. Long ago, he says, the divine craftsman made two great bows, one for Shiva and one for Vishnu. The gods wanted to know which was stronger, and a contest broke out. In his telling, one great roar from Vishnu left Shiva's bow slack, and the gods of the story judged Vishnu the stronger. Shiva's bow passed to the kings of Videha; that's the one Rama broke. Vishnu's bow came down through Parashurama's own family, and here it is. String this one, he tells Rama, fit an arrow to it, and then we fight. Dasharatha begs. You're a brahmin. You laid down your weapons. You gave the earth away. Spare my son. Parashurama doesn't even answer the king. He speaks only to Rama. One Rama is facing another, and in later tradition, both are Vishnu come down to earth.
screen: `A FIRE NO ONE CAN LOOK AT.` · `THE SON OF JAMADAGNI.` · `TWO BOWS: SHIVA'S AND VISHNU'S.` · `STRING THIS ONE, THEN WE FIGHT.` · then, large: `ONE RAMA FACES ANOTHER.`

segments.voice: Think of a challenge that came at you lately, from someone older, louder or very sure of themselves, and don't answer it yet; just notice the jaw, the shoulders, the belly. On each breath out, let one of those places soften: not giving in, just making room to answer well.
Parashurama's challenge. The axe-bearing son of Jamadagni meets Rama on the road home and holds out Vishnu's bow: string it, and then we fight.
Your line: string this one, then we fight. Tomorrow, Rama answers. That's day five hundred twelve.

howItsDone: Hindu tradition counts Parashurama among Vishnu's ten avatars, usually listed sixth, and his birth is marked on Parashurama Jayanti in the spring month of Vaishakha.

original.note: Sanskrit paraśurāma: Rama with the paraśu, the axe. Valmiki mostly calls him Jamadagnya, son of Jamadagni.

trapdoor: what you thought: Parashurama is just an angry sage.
what it means: he's a brahmin warrior carrying Vishnu's bow, come to test the prince who broke Shiva's.
what a scholar hears: in the later lists of ten avatars he's usually sixth and Rama seventh, so this road meeting reads as one avatar meeting the next.

Parashurama.meaning: Rama with the axe; later tradition counts him an avatar of Vishnu

Bhrigu.meaning: an ancient sage whose family Parashurama belongs to

Videha.meaning: Janaka's kingdom, where Shiva's bow was kept

notes: Sarga numbers follow the common (vulgate) numbering; the Baroda critical edition differs. Please confirm.
Valmiki mostly names him Jamadagnya or Bhargava Rama; the name Parashurama is used here as the index does. Confirm framing as 'later tradition calls him'.
The contest of the two bows: the script says Vishnu's roar (humkara) made Shiva's bow slack. Confirm detail.
Avatar lists vary; 'usually sixth' is softened deliberately.
The story of his war on the kshatriyas is given only in outline (no count of twenty-one times).
Reviewer: 'a king killed his father' softened to 'killed in a feud with a royal house'; traditions differ on whether Kartavirya Arjuna or his sons killed Jamadagni. Confirm.

Reviewer: the bow contest ranks Vishnu over Shiva. It is in Valmiki (Bala 75), but Shaiva listeners may hear it as sectarian; the script now frames it as Parashurama's telling. A Keeper should confirm the framing is fair to Shaiva traditions.
